headline: Trump’s AI Gambit Fuels Wild Thanksgiving Week on Wall Street
author: Emma Haidar

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- The message from Washington this week was unmistakable: America must do whatever it takes to win the artificial-intelligence race with China, and the government is prepared to intervene to make it happen.
Most Read from Bloomberg
A jittery Wall Street has cheered the message. Yet the wild swings in financial markets show the limits of investor conviction.

President Donald Trump's intervention to bring Jensen Huang back to Nvidia Corp. restored to the helm not just one of the biggest AI evangelists but one of the chief financiers of its expansion. Technology stocks soared, sank and rallied again, with a 1.6% jump in the S&P 500 Friday capping a week of gains across risk assets.

The recent turbulence, which Trump acknowledged Thursday had briefly left him concerned, was an unusually intense bout of the volatility that has gripped Wall Street for months as the financial and economic stakes of the AI boom have grown.

"There was a tacit admission – or maybe not even so tacit – that Nvidia's too big to fail, Jensen is too big to fail, and if you're well enough connected with the powers that be, you'll get bailed out to some extent," said Steve Sosnick, chief strategist at Interactive Brokers.
The euphoria over Huang's return had barely lasted a day before stocks started sliding again, while fresh tariff threats from the Trump administration added to market swings.

An average of 21 billion shares changed hands daily in the first three sessions, the busiest start to Thanksgiving week in Bloomberg data going back to 2008. The Nasdaq 100 Index had alternated between weekly gains and losses of more than 3% for four straight weeks, something not seen since July 2022.

Through Wednesday's close, a gauge of expected volatility in the Nasdaq 100 had averaged 33 in November, putting it on course for its highest monthly reading since April 2022 and the highest for any November since the global financial crisis. Relative to a diversified portfolio of global stocks, bonds and commodities, US equities have been this volatile only once before since the pandemic, going by 30-day measures of realized volatility.

At the heart of the whiplash is a question that even the full political weight of the US government cannot answer: Who will emerge as the winners and losers from one of the biggest investment booms in history? The prospect of higher borrowing costs only compounds the dilemma, raising the bar for those investments to pay off.

Uncertainty over future demand for all the computing capacity being built is making markets particularly sensitive to incremental news, said Michael Reynolds, vice president of investment strategy at Glenmede. "Every time we get a new piece of information on a headline here, investors are updating their priors."

That uncertainty is making investors more discriminating about where they put their money. At RWA Wealth Partners, which has about $22 billion under management, Chief Investment Officer JP Powers said investors are shying away from specialized cloud-computing providers and diversifying into sectors such as health care and consumer staples.

"If you just sat back for the week and looked at the weekly returns, you'd probably be happy to have missed some of these violent swings here and just stuck it out in the Dow, more value-oriented names," Powers said.

For now, the gyrations on Wall Street stand in contrast to the strength of the American economy. Data this week showed gross domestic product expanded at a 4.3% annualized pace in the third quarter. The AI spending spree, household wealth, resilient consumption and government outlays have all helped sustain the expansion.

While a prolonged slump in stocks could take a toll on consumer spending, the more immediate concern for investors is that the economy remains too hot to warrant monetary relief. Traders are all-in betting on an interest-rate increase from the Federal Reserve next month, further complicating the economics of the AI buildout.

The flip side is that the very investment boom unnerving Wall Street is helping insulate the economy against a downturn, according to Justin Bergner, a portfolio manager at Gabelli Funds. "We also have a much stronger economic engine in AI than we have had supporting past cycles," he said.

Investors may not need to resolve the question of who ultimately profits from AI to make money in the stock market over the next few months. The recent bouts of turbulence have left hedge funds with some of their lowest net equity exposure in years, a cohort of systematic traders heavily short and demand for protection against losses elevated. In that scenario, even a modest improvement in sentiment could unleash a substantial wave of buying.
Bergner, for one, bought Nvidia shares last Friday afternoon after Huang's departure pushed the stock to recent lows, betting on a rebound.
"I am looking selectively at buying into some tech names like I did with the Nvidia position, just based on the notion that tech feels very heavily sold in the market," he said.
